name: ip
summary: Show and configure network interfaces, IP addresses and routes (replaces ifconfig and route).
compat: ifconfig (net-tools) is deprecated and missing on many systems. Changes made with ip are temporary; NetworkManager, systemd-networkd or ifupdown own the permanent configuration.

examples.title: Show addresses on all interfaces
examples.explain: Look for 'inet' (IPv4) and 'inet6' lines under each interface. 'state UP' means the link is up; lo is the loopback interface (127.0.0.1).

examples.title: Compact one-line-per-interface view
examples.explain: Brief output: name, state, addresses. Quick to scan on a board with several interfaces.

examples.title: Show the routing table and default gateway
examples.explain: The 'default via X' line is your gateway. No default route means you can reach the local network but not the internet.

examples.title: Bring an interface up
examples.explain: Enables the link (e.g. eth0). It does not assign an address; DHCP or a static address is configured separately.
examples.warning: Changing interfaces on a remote machine can cut your own SSH connection. Use a local console when experimenting.

name: ss
summary: List sockets: which ports are listening and which connections are open (replaces netstat).

install.note: BusyBox systems often only have netstat.

compat: Process names (-p) for other users' sockets are only shown to root. On BusyBox, netstat -ltn gives similar output.

examples.title: Listening TCP ports
examples.explain: Local Address 0.0.0.0:22 or [::]:22 = listening on all interfaces; 127.0.0.1:631 = only reachable from this machine.

examples.title: Listening ports with the owning process
examples.explain: Adds UDP (-u) and the process name/PID (-p). Answers 'what program is listening on port 8080?'.
examples.warning: sudo is only needed to see processes of other users; the command does not change anything.

examples.title: Established TCP connections
examples.explain: Shows current connections with local and remote address:port.

name: ping
summary: Check whether a host is reachable and how long round trips take.
compat: Many networks and hosts block ICMP, so no reply does not always mean the host is down. Without -c, Linux ping runs until Ctrl+C.

examples.title: Send four pings
examples.explain: Each reply shows time= in milliseconds; the summary shows packet loss. 'Name or service not known' is a DNS problem; 'Network is unreachable' means no route.

examples.title: Separate DNS problems from connectivity problems
examples.explain: If pinging an IP address works but a host name fails, the network is fine and name resolution (DNS) is the problem.

name: curl
summary: Transfer data from or to a URL; test HTTP APIs and download files.

install.note: Missing in some minimal images; BusyBox provides wget instead.

compat: Never pipe a downloaded script straight into a shell (curl ... | sh) without reading it first.

examples.title: Download a file, keeping its remote name
examples.explain: -O saves to a file named like the last part of the URL; -L follows redirects; -f fails on HTTP errors instead of saving the error page.
examples.warning: Overwrites a local file with the same name. Verify the published checksum afterwards (sha256sum <file>).
options: Save with the remote file name

examples.title: Show only the response headers
examples.explain: The first line has the status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 301 redirect).

examples.title: Send JSON to an API
examples.explain: -d sends the body; -H adds a header. Single quotes keep the JSON's double quotes intact.
examples.warning: POST requests usually change data on the server. Point it at a test endpoint you control.

name: wget
summary: Download files over HTTP/HTTPS/FTP, with resume support.
compat: BusyBox wget supports basic downloads and -O, -c, -q; many GNU options are missing.

examples.title: Download a file
examples.explain: Saves into the current directory. If the name exists, GNU wget saves as name.1 instead of overwriting.

examples.title: Resume an interrupted download
examples.explain: Continues a partial file instead of starting over, useful for large SDK or image downloads.

examples.title: Choose the output file name
examples.explain: -O - writes to standard output instead.
options: Write the download to this file

name: ssh
summary: Open a secure shell on a remote machine or board, or run one command there.

install.note: Embedded targets often run Dropbear as a small SSH server.

compat: The first connection asks you to confirm the host key fingerprint. 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED' after reflashing a board is expected; remove the old key with ssh-keygen -R <host>. On any other machine treat it as a possible attack.

examples.title: Log in to a remote machine
examples.explain: Type exit or press Ctrl+D to leave. 'Connection refused' = no SSH server listening; 'Permission denied' = wrong user, password or key.

examples.title: Use a non-standard port
examples.explain: -p chooses the server port (default 22).

examples.title: Run one command remotely
examples.explain: Quote the remote command so the whole thing is executed on the remote side rather than by your local shell.

name: ssh-keygen
summary: Create SSH key pairs for password-less login and manage known host keys.
compat: Share only the .pub file. The private key (without .pub) must stay secret and readable only by you (chmod 600).

examples.title: Create a new key pair
examples.explain: Prompts for a file name (default ~/.ssh/id_ed25519) and an optional passphrase. The comment, often your e-mail, helps you recognise the key later.
examples.warning: If a key with the chosen name exists you are asked before it is overwritten. Overwriting a key you already use locks you out of servers that trust it.
options: Comment stored in the public key

examples.title: Install your public key on a remote machine
examples.explain: Appends your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the remote host so future logins do not ask for the password.

examples.title: Forget an outdated host key
examples.explain: Removes the stored key for <host> from ~/.ssh/known_hosts (a backup is saved as known_hosts.old). Use it after reinstalling or reflashing a device you control.
options: Remove the host's keys from known_hosts

name: scp
summary: Copy files to or from a remote machine over SSH.
compat: Recent OpenSSH scp uses the SFTP protocol; if a small embedded SSH server lacks SFTP, add -O to use the legacy protocol.

examples.title: Copy a local file to a remote directory
examples.explain: Typical for deploying a cross-compiled binary to a board. The colon separates host from remote path.
examples.warning: A remote file with the same name is overwritten without asking.

examples.title: Copy a file from the remote machine
examples.explain: The trailing . means 'into the current directory'.
examples.warning: Overwrites a local file with the same name.

name: rsync
summary: Efficiently synchronise directories locally or over SSH, copying only what changed.

install.note: Must be installed on both ends for remote copies.

compat: A trailing slash on the source matters: src/ copies the contents of src, src copies the directory itself.

examples.title: Preview a sync with a dry run
examples.explain: Lists what would be transferred without copying anything. Always do this first.
options: Archive mode: recursive, keep permissions, times, links
Show what would happen, change nothing

examples.title: Sync a directory to a remote machine
examples.explain: Copies only new or changed files. Re-running it after a small change is fast.
examples.warning: Changed files at the destination are overwritten. Run with --dry-run first.

examples.title: Mirror exactly, deleting extra files at the destination
examples.explain: Makes the destination identical to the source, removing files that only exist at the destination.
examples.warning: --delete permanently removes destination files that are not in the source. Swapping source and destination, or forgetting a trailing slash, can wipe the wrong side. Run the identical command with --dry-run first.
options: Delete destination files missing from the source

name: dig
summary: Query DNS servers to see what a host name resolves to.
compat: getent hosts <name> is always available and uses the same resolver as normal programs (including /etc/hosts), while dig asks DNS servers directly.

examples.title: Short answer: just the addresses
examples.explain: Empty output means no A record was found.

examples.title: Resolve the way ordinary programs do
examples.explain: Consults /etc/hosts and DNS according to /etc/nsswitch.conf. If this works but dig fails (or vice versa), the difference is in that configuration.
